latest_nl_proof:
Fix n = 2. Then a sign sequence has length n - 1 = 1, so it consists of a single entry, and that entry must be either +1 or -1. Therefore the only sign sequences of length 1 are (+1) and (-1).

Each of these sequences is alternating: a sequence of length 1 has no adjacent pair of entries, so there is no possible violation of alternation.

Now consider the counting function f. For a sign sequence s = (s_1), f(s) counts the permutations (a_1,a_2) of {1,2} such that s_1(a_2-a_1) > 0. The only permutations of {1,2} are (1,2) and (2,1).

For s = (+1), the condition is a_2 - a_1 > 0. This is true for (1,2), since 2 - 1 = 1 > 0, and false for (2,1), since 1 - 2 = -1 < 0. Hence f((+1)) = 1.

For s = (-1), the condition is -(a_2-a_1) > 0, equivalently a_2 - a_1 < 0. This is true for (2,1), since 1 - 2 = -1 < 0, and false for (1,2), since 2 - 1 = 1 > 0. Hence f((-1)) = 1.

So each of the two sign sequences is satisfied by exactly one permutation of {1,2}. Since (+1) and (-1) are the only sign sequences of length 1, the maximum possible value of the counting function is 1, and both of these sequences attain it. Therefore, when n = 2, both sign sequences maximize the counting function.
role_in_parent: Provides the base case for the induction on n.
statement_nl: When n = 2, the two sign sequences of length 1 are (+1) and (-1). Each of them is alternating, and each is satisfied by exactly one permutation of {1,2}. Hence for n = 2 both sign sequences maximize the counting function.

domain_restrictions: n is a natural number, and here n equals 2.
Sign sequences under discussion have length 1.
The only sign sequences mentioned are plus one and minus one.
Permutations are taken of the set {1,2}.
The counting function is evaluated on sign sequences of length 1.
Maximize means among all sign sequences of the relevant length, ties allowed.
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: In the special case n equals 2, there are exactly two sign sequences of length 1, plus one and minus one. Both are alternating, and each has exactly one satisfying permutation of {1,2}. Therefore both sequences achieve the maximum possible value of the counting function for that case.
quantifier_order: Consider the two sign sequences of length 1, namely plus one and minus one.
For each such sign sequence, it is alternating.
For each such sign sequence, there exists exactly one permutation of {1,2} that satisfies it.
Therefore each of the two sign sequences attains the maximum value of the counting function for n equal to 2.
